summary: A near-verbatim copy of NADF-123, in which the North American Directory Forum sets out how entries are named in the public portions of the North American Directory for c=US. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 1255 and RFC 1417.

eli5.summary: This is a naming rulebook for a big directory in the United States. Newer versions replaced it.

questions: how are entries named in the c=us directory
what is the naming scheme for c=us
how are organizations named in the directory
subtitle: A hierarchical naming scheme for the North American directory.

tldr.problem: As Directory services grew, there was a need for a consistent, hierarchical scheme to name entries in the North American Directory. The scheme had to leverage existing naming authorities and provide enough namespace to avoid collisions.
tldr.mechanism: The naming scheme organizes entries into four components: civil naming (based on geography and political boundaries), organizational naming, ADDMD (Administrative Directory Management Domain) naming, and application naming. Civil naming is structured at national, regional (state), and local (populated place) levels, with optimized forms to support efficient searching.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1218 was replaced by RFC 1255 and RFC 1417, which updated the naming rules as directory practices evolved.

today: RFC 1255 and RFC 1417 replaced this RFC, updating the North American Directory naming scheme.

sections.title: Overview of Directory Naming
sections.content:
The North American Directory is a public Directory service based on the CCITT X.500 Recommendations. It organizes millions of entries representing people, organizations, and systems. Like a postal service, it needs a consistent way to name and address every entry so they can be found reliably.

The challenge is that names must be globally unique (to avoid collisions), drawn from existing naming authorities (to leverage what already exists), and user-friendly enough to support searches and lookups. This RFC proposes a solution built on four naming components: civil, organizational, ADDMD, and application naming.
sections.eli5: The RFC explains how to name things in a big directory for North America. Each name has to be unique, like house addresses that no two houses share. It uses government names for states and cities to make sure the system works with real-world geography.

sections.title: Design Principles
sections.content:
The scheme uses a civil naming universe based on real-world geography and civil authority. It recognizes that Distinguished Names (the administrative names used in the directory) are not the same as user-friendly names. The scheme keeps them separate: Distinguished Names are unique, while other attributes can hold friendly aliases.

For example, an organization might have the Distinguished Name organizationName is Performance Systems International, but other attributes could store organizationName is PSI, making it easier to search for.

The scheme also introduces Relative Distinguished Names (RDNs), which are the parts that make a name unique at each level. Each RDN must avoid collisions with siblings and provide enough namespace for growth.
sections.eli5: The scheme separates two kinds of names: the official unique names (Distinguished Names) and nicknames people use to search. You might file something under "Performance Systems International" officially, but people can search for "PSI" too.

sections.title: Civil Naming at Three Levels
sections.content:
Civil naming reflects real-world geography and political structure:

National level contains three kinds of entries: States and state-equivalents (using FIPS 5 names like California), organizations with national standing (using ANSI alphanumeric names), and ADDMD operators (directory service providers).

Regional level (within each state) contains populated places (using FIPS 55 place names like Hartford, Connecticut) and organizations with regional standing (registered with a state Secretary of State or equivalent).

Local level (within each populated place) contains residential persons, organizations with local standing (registered with county or city authorities), and MHS (Message Handling System) distribution lists.
sections.eli5: The directory is organized like a map. At the top is the whole United States. Below that are states. Below each state are cities and towns. Below those are individual people and businesses. Each level uses real government names and codes to stay organized.

sections.title: Optimized Civil Naming
sections.content:
Optimized civil naming places copies of some entries at higher levels to speed up searches. For example, an organization with regional standing (like a business licensed in California) would normally live under that state. But a copy can be listed directly under c=US with a multi-valued RDN combining both the organization name and the state, so a single search can find it without first searching all states.

Similarly, a residential person can be listed under a state as well as under their specific city, with attributes like commonName is Marshall T. Rose, localityName is City of Mountain View, allowing faster lookup.

A new attribute type, nadfSearchGuide, indicates which optimizations are in effect for efficient searching by directory systems.
sections.eli5: Instead of always searching down through all the levels, some entries are copied to higher levels with clues about where they really belong. Like marking both the city and state on an address so you can find it faster.

sections.title: Organizational, ADDMD, and Application Naming
sections.content:
Organizational naming is left to individual organizations. They may use organizational units (like departments) to structure their internal directory. This allows each company to organize itself as it sees fit.

ADDMD naming (Administrative Directory Management Domain) defines how directory service providers structure entries under their control. The NADF coordinates registration of ADDMD names but leaves internal structure to the providers.

Application naming covers OSI application entities, devices, and electronic data interchange (EDI) users. The RFC requires that application entities be immediately subordinate to application process objects, and that they use a specific nadfApplicationEntity object class with mandatory supportedApplicationContext attributes for interoperability.
sections.eli5: Companies can organize their own departments however they like. Directory service providers (the companies running the directory) organize themselves however they want. And special computer applications can register themselves with required information to prove they work together.

sections.title: Schema Definitions and Examples
sections.content:
The RFC includes formal schema definitions in ASN.1 for all the new object classes and attributes. These define usStateOrEquivalent, usPlace, usCounty, usOrganization, nadfApplicationEntity, and nadfADDMD, along with attribute types like fipsStateNumericCode, fipsPlaceNumericCode, and ansiOrgNumericCode.

Examples show complete Distinguished Names, like c=US, l=California, o=Government for the State of California's government office, and c=US, l=California, l=City of Mountain View, o=The Tied House for a local business in Mountain View.
sections.eli5: The RFC includes a formal definition in a special language that directory systems use to understand the structure. It also shows real examples of what finished names look like for different types of entries.
